lesson.title: The agent loop
lesson.subtitle: Ask, run, add, repeat, and know when to stop

chapters.label: The loop and a scripted model
When a step fails, and the lab

scenes.visual: A list: It never stopped; Call, result, call…; Until the battery died.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: I tested an agent that a student wrote, and it never stopped! Call, result, call, result. No answer, ever, until the battery died.

scenes.animation: The Darsi mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: the agent loop in Python, and how to make it stop.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: An agent is a loop around a model. Ask the model for its next output. If it’s an answer, you’re done. If it’s a call, run the tool, add both to the history, and ask again.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: SCRIPT = ['weather{"place":"Kafi"}', …
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: But the Python sandbox has no language model inside. So in your code, a scripted model stands in: a function that returns what a model would write, from a list. It’s not intelligent, and we say so. It lets you test your loop.

scenes.visual: A list: The request; Each call; Each result; All read again, every turn.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The history is everything so far: the request, then each call and its result, in order. A real model reads it all on every turn: that’s its only memory. Your loop builds it, one turn at a time.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: for step in range(limit): …
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Here’s the loop. For each step, ask the model. No curly bracket means an answer, so return it. Otherwise, run the tool, and add both to the history.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Why for step in range, and not while true? Because a model can get stuck, calling tool after tool without answering. A step limit is a promise: after four steps, the loop stops, whatever the model writes.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The script only ever returns calls, never an answer, and the limit is four. What does the agent return?

scenes.visual: A list: Four steps, then stop; Tell the person; Never hide a stop.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Stopped, after four steps. That’s the step limit doing its job. In a real app, you’d also tell the person: I couldn’t finish this. Never hide a stop.

scenes.visual: A list: route: Kafi to Dala; Then weather in Dala; Saturday: “no school”; A reminder set anyway.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Some goals need two tools. The trip from Kafi to Dala calls route, then weather, using the first result. But a step can fail. Asked for six B’s first lesson on Saturday, Darsi Tiny got no school, and still set a reminder.

scenes.visual: A list: Guess the tools, watch the plan; Run the Saturday goal; Your loop: stop on an error.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In the lab, guess which tools a goal needs, then watch Darsi Tiny plan and call them. Run the Saturday goal, and see the failed step. Your loop could stop there, with a check in code.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Your loop passes every test with the scripted model. What have you shown?

scenes.visual: Summary points: Ask, run, add, repeat; A step limit stops it; A script tests your code.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask, run, add, repeat · A step limit stops it · A script tests your code
scenes.narration: That your loop works, for the outputs you tested. Remember: the loop asks the model, runs its calls and builds the history. A step limit stops a stuck model. And a scripted model tests your code, not the model.

scenes.visual: A list: A model, a tool and a loop; The model reads a script card; Count, and stop at four; A script that never answers.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: play the loop with two friends. One is the model, reading from a script card. One is the tool. You are the loop: count the steps, and stop at four. Then try a script that never answers.

checkpoints.prompt: The script only ever returns calls, and the limit is 4. What does agent() return?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the for loop runs four steps at most, then reaches return “Stopped”. The model can’t keep it going.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the step limit ends the loop after four steps, and the agent returns “Stopped”.

checkpoints.prompt: Your loop passes every test with a scripted model. What have you shown?

options.text: That the real model will behave the same
That your loop works for the outputs you tested
That every tool gives the right result

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a script tests your code. A real model writes new things, wrong calls and stuck loops included, so your code must handle those too.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a script only tests your code for the outputs in it. The real model can write things your script never did.
